title: Nucleus overload guide (part. 4): Reps, sets and frequency schemes
summary: NH corrects an earlier confusion: nucleus overload does not mean 40-60 rep sets, only that the work is never challenging. He gives his rep, set and frequency schemes for traps, triceps, neck, calves and lats, and explains that progression should come from adding reps and sets rather than weight.
claims: In part 1 he mistakenly sounded like nucleus overload means 40-60 reps per set; it does not, that range is a waste of time
The only rule of nucleus overload is staying in intensity windows that are not challenging; a challenging movement is not nucleus overload
Two ways to do it: lower reps sandbagged with reps in the tank, or a load that brings failure around 20-25 reps where about 95% of reps were not challenging
With zero-intensity very high reps the muscle recovers during the set, so it can go almost forever and does nothing
His hypertrophy striking range is 2-15 reps, preferably 6-12; for nucleus overload he goes 4-25
Warm up for nucleus overload as well; do not jump straight in
He gives concepts rather than protocols so viewers find what works best for them
He uses nucleus overload for neck, lats, triceps, calves and traps
Traps: 6-20 reps, rep counts fluctuate freely, e.g. 135 lb for 20 shrugs up to 275 lb for 6
Weighted stretch is amazing for the traps; he shrugs or does weighted stretch every time he pulls
Traps nucleus overload 2-4 times a week; they recover fast and never fail structurally
Pick muscles for nucleus overload that are not prone to structural failure, to avoid injury
Traps get his highest set count, often 8-10 sets, since a small range of motion and fast recovery make tonnage easy
Triceps: sometimes 30 reps with bands, or 6-10 on behind-the-head extensions; only 3-4 sets because his small weak triceps cannot handle much volume without hurting his presses
Neck: avoid high-intensity rep ranges to prevent injury; 4-7 sets, 8-12 or 10-15 reps in every direction, fixed at 3 times a week
Calves respond very well to high volume; bodyweight up to 25-30 reps, weighted 6-10 or 8-12, the two feeding each other
Any nucleus overload scheme should have a strength-work counterpart for that muscle
Lats: DB pullovers at 4-12 reps, preferably 5-7, because higher reps shift the feel to the long head of the triceps; 3 to 7-8 sets
Nucleus overload can be weighted, but the load must never be challenging
Progress nucleus overload by adding reps or sets at the same weight, not weight; across many sets one extra rep each adds a lot of tonnage
Pushing intensity turns nucleus overload into strength work or a back-off set
Add weight only when added reps become irrelevant or you run out of sets to superset it into
exercises: 5-7 reps; stop when triceps take over
